prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Willie had a stubborn wart upon his middle toe. Regardless, though, of what he tried the wart refused to go. So Willie went and visited his family foot physician, who instantly agreed it was a stubborn wart condition. The doctor tried to squeeze the wart. He tried to twist and turn it. He tried to scrape and shave the wart. He tried to boil and burn it. He poked it with a pair of tongs. He pulled it with his tweezers. He held it under heat lamps, and he crammed it into freezers. Regrettably these treatments were of very little use. He looked at it and sputtered, “Ach! I cannot get it loose!” “I’ll have to get some bigger tools to help me to dissect it. I’ll need to pound and pummel it, bombard it and inject it.” He whacked it with a hammer, and he yanked it with a wrench. He seared it with a welding torch despite the nasty stench. He drilled it with a power drill. He wrestled it with pliers. He zapped it with a million volts from large electric wires. He blasted it with gamma rays, besieged it with corrosives, assaulted it with dynamite and nuclear explosives. He hit the wart with everything, but when the smoke had cleared, poor Willie’s stubborn wart remained, and Willie’d disappeared.

outputs.L2:
Willie had a persistent growth on the middle toe of his foot. No matter what remedy he attempted, however, the growth simply wouldn't leave. Eventually, Willie sought out the podiatrist his family always used, and the doctor immediately confirmed this was indeed a particularly obstinate case.

The physician attempted to compress it. Next he attempted rotating and manipulating it from different angles. He attempted scraping and shaving away at it. He tried applying both boiling heat and burning it directly. He jabbed at it using tongs. He attempted extraction with tweezers. He exposed it to heat lamps, then alternated by freezing it solid. Unfortunately, none of these approaches yielded results. Examining it with frustration, he exclaimed, "Blast it! This thing won't budge!"

"I suppose I'll need heavier equipment to tackle this properly. Time to hammer and crush it, blast it and inject it with something."

He struck it repeatedly using a hammer, then attempted prying it loose with a wrench. Despite the awful odor, he applied a welding torch to burn through it. He bored into it with a power drill. He grappled with it using pliers. He subjected it to a million volts through massive electrical cables.

He hit it with gamma radiation, doused it in corrosive chemicals, and finally attacked it with both dynamite and nuclear weapons. He threw absolutely everything at that wart—yet once the dust settled, the stubborn growth was still firmly in place on the toe.

Willie himself, unfortunately, was nowhere to be found.
outputs.L3:
# The Stubborn Wart

Willie had a wart on his middle toe. It was small, unassuming, and utterly refused to leave. He had tried everything he could think of—pressing on it, picking at it, willing it away through sheer determination—but the wart remained, stubborn and unmoved by his efforts.

Finally, exasperated, Willie decided to seek professional help. He made an appointment with his family's foot physician, a man who had been treating Willie's family for years and had seen his fair share of unusual cases. After a thorough examination, the doctor delivered his verdict: this was, without question, one of the most stubborn warts he had ever encountered in his career.

Undeterred, the doctor began working through his standard arsenal of treatments. He squeezed it. He twisted it. He scraped at it with careful precision. He tried boiling the affected area and then, in stark contrast, freezing it solid. Each method was applied with the confidence of years of experience—and each method failed completely. The wart sat on Willie's toe, seemingly amused by the doctor's efforts.

Frustration began to creep into the physician's demeanor. If gentle, conventional methods wouldn't work, perhaps something more forceful would. The doctor's toolkit expanded dramatically. He reached for a hammer, thinking a firm strike might dislodge the stubborn growth. When that failed, he tried a wrench, attempting to twist it free with mechanical leverage. A welding torch came next, followed by a power drill, and then—in a move that suggested the doctor's judgment had perhaps become clouded by sheer determination—electric shocks were administered directly to the toe. Nothing worked. The wart remained, impervious to every escalating attempt at removal.

By this point, the doctor's frustration had transformed into something bordering on obsession. Conventional medicine had failed him, mechanical intervention had failed him, and even electricity had proven useless. There was only one direction left to go: total, overwhelming force. In a final, desperate bid to eliminate the wart once and for all, the doctor brought out the heaviest tools available to him—gamma rays and explosives, weapons capable of altering matter itself.

The results were catastrophic, though not in the way anyone had intended. The wart, against all logic and scientific reasoning, remained completely unaffected. Willie, however, did not fare so well. In a flash of light and force, Willie himself vanished entirely, leaving no trace behind—nothing but an empty room, a bewildered doctor, and a wart that, presumably, was still exactly where it had always been.
outputs.L4:
# The Wart

Willie Thompson noticed the wart on his big toe on a Tuesday. By Thursday, it had become an obsession. It wasn't a particularly large wart, nor an especially painful one, but it was *stubborn*, and Willie had never been able to tolerate stubbornness in inanimate objects—or in his own body.

He made an appointment with Dr. Heinrich Bloch, a podiatrist recommended by his neighbor for being "thorough."

"Just a common wart," Dr. Bloch said, peering through his spectacles. "We'll start simple."

Simple meant squeezing. Dr. Bloch pinched the wart between his thumb and forefinger with considerable force, as though trying to pop a particularly resistant grape. Willie yelped, but the wart remained, smug and unbothered.

"No matter," said Dr. Bloch. "Freezing, then."

He produced a canister of liquid nitrogen and applied it liberally to Willie's toe. The wart turned white, then returned to its normal pink hue within the hour, seemingly amused by the whole ordeal.

Dr. Bloch's brow furrowed. "We shall need to be more aggressive."

The following week, he arrived with a small hammer. "Sometimes," he explained, "blunt trauma disrupts the cellular structure." He tapped Willie's toe—gently at first, then with increasing enthusiasm—until Willie was hopping around the office clutching his foot and questioning his life choices. The wart, for its part, seemed unbothered, perhaps even invigorated.

"A drill," Dr. Bloch murmured, more to himself than to Willie. "We'll bore it out directly."

Willie should have left then. He did not. Something about Dr. Bloch's unwavering confidence—or perhaps sheer stubbornness matching his own—kept him in that chair as the doctor fetched a power drill from a back closet. The procedure that followed involved considerable screaming, a small fire, and ultimately, no reduction in wart size whatsoever.

"I don't understand it," Dr. Bloch said, wiping sweat from his forehead. "This wart defies conventional medicine."

"Perhaps," Willie suggested weakly, "we could just leave it alone?"

Dr. Bloch looked at him as though he'd suggested abandoning modern civilization altogether. "Nonsense. We simply need more force."

The dynamite arrived the following Monday. Dr. Bloch had somehow acquired three sticks from a construction site down the road, and he arranged them around Willie's foot with the meticulous care of a man building a diorama. "Now this," he said confidently, "should do the trick."

Willie, to his eternal regret, was assured that the blast radius would be "minimal" and that Dr. Bloch had "read extensively" on the subject. The explosion took out a wall of the office, several instruments, and Dr. Bloch's eyebrows, but when the smoke cleared, Willie's toe—badly singed and undoubtedly worse for wear—still bore the wart, defiant as ever.

By this point, word had spread through the small town about the doctor's unusual methods, and most sensible people would have sought a second opinion. But Willie was not most sensible people, and Dr. Bloch had developed what could only be described as a personal vendetta against the wart itself.

"I have a contact," Dr. Bloch said one evening, his eyes gleaming with the particular madness of a man who has lost all perspective, "at a research facility. They have... other options."

"Other options?"

"Nuclear options."

Willie should have run. Instead, three weeks later, he found himself standing in a decommissioned testing facility in the desert, his foot secured to a metal platform while Dr. Bloch, wearing what appeared to be a hazmat suit purchased from a costume shop, made final adjustments to a device that hummed with unsettling energy.

"This will definitely work," Dr. Bloch assured him through his helmet's small window. "Nothing survives a controlled nuclear detonation. Nothing."

The countdown began. Willie's last thought, as the device activated, was that perhaps—just perhaps—simply ignoring the wart might have been the wiser course of action.

The explosion was visible from three counties away. When the dust settled and the radiation cleared enough for investigators to approach, they found the testing platform vaporized, a crater where the facility once stood, and absolutely no trace of Willie Thompson.

They did, however, find one thing: sitting atop a small mound of glass-melted sand, perfectly intact and seemingly untouched by the blast, was a single wart.

Dr. Bloch, who had survived by some cosmic joke of physics, stared at it in disbelief.

"Well," he said finally, adjusting his cracked helmet. "I suppose we'll need something stronger."
outputs.L5:
# Willie's Resolve

Willie had never been one to back down from a challenge. Growing up in a small town where opportunities were scarce, he learned early that success wouldn't come easily to someone like him. The odds seemed stacked against him from the very beginning—limited resources, few connections, and a community that often doubted his ambitions.

Regardless of these obstacles, Willie pursued his dreams with a quiet determination that surprised even those closest to him. He worked double shifts at the local mill during the day and studied late into the night, teaching himself skills that would eventually open doors he never thought possible. Friends questioned his sanity. Family members worried he was setting himself up for disappointment. Still, he pressed forward.

The turning point came not from some dramatic stroke of luck, but from years of consistent, unglamorous effort. The small business he eventually built started in his garage, funded by savings he'd scraped together penny by penny. The early days were difficult—canceled orders, equipment failures, and moments when quitting seemed like the only reasonable option.

But Willie understood something fundamental about perseverance: the path forward rarely announces itself clearly. Regardless of setbacks, he adjusted his approach, learned from failures, and refused to let temporary defeats become permanent conclusions.

Today, when people ask Willie about the secret to his success, he shrugs off any suggestion that he possessed some special talent or unusual luck. Instead, he speaks about the value of showing up consistently, regardless of how difficult circumstances might seem in the moment. The lesson he offers isn't complicated, but it's one that requires genuine commitment: obstacles will always exist, but they don't have to define the outcome.

His story serves as a reminder that resilience often matters more than raw talent, and that regardless of where someone starts, the choices they make each day ultimately shape where they end up.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a funny rhyming poem, Shel Silverstein-style, about a kid with a wart that won't go away no matter what the doctor tries.
counterfactuals.output:
**Wilbur's Wart**

I've got a wart on my left thumb,
It's been there since the world begun
(or so it feels—it's been a while,
since spring, or fall, or possibly April).

The doctor poked it, froze it, zapped it,
Wrapped it, taped it, sprayed it, capped it,
Gave me pills the size of trucks,
Rubbed on cream that smelled like duck.

He burned it off on a Tuesday noon—
It grew right back by Wednesday afternoon!
He cut it out with a tiny knife,
It came back bigger, full of life!

We tried the folk cures, one by one:
Toad juice dabbed at rising sun,
A penny buried 'neath the moon,
Duct tape worn from May to June.

Grandma said to kiss a frog,
So I did (behind the log),
The frog just stared with knowing eyes
And whispered, "Kid, that wart's my prize."

Turns out warts are kind of clever—
Mine's decided to live forever.
It's got a name now: Reginald.
We're getting kind of close, if I'm honest.

He listens when I've had a bad day,
Doesn't mind when it's cold in May,
So doc, don't cut, and doc, don't freeze—
Reginald and I? We're a package deal, please.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a darkly humorous children's-style poem where a doctor uses increasingly absurd and extreme methods to remove a stubborn wart, ending in an ironic twist.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wart That Wouldn't Go

There once was a wart on the tip of my thumb,
Stubborn and proud as a general's drum.
"I'll fix it!" said Doc, with a glint in his eye,
"No wart is too tough, and no method too sly!"

He started off simple—a dab of clear paint,
A liquid that promised (through label complaint)
To freeze off the wart in a week, maybe two.
The wart just sat there and grew, and it grew.

"No matter!" said Doc, "I've got other tricks!"
He came at me next with some tweezers and picks,
Then sandpaper, scissors, a tiny toy saw—
The wart didn't flinch. It just sat there in awe.

He brought in a laser (the kind for the moon),
A blowtorch, a hammer, a wee-tiny spoon.
He tried leeches and lightning and lemon-lime spray,
The wart settled in like it planned on a stay.

"I'll end this!" cried Doc, now unhinged and quite wild,
"No wart makes a fool of a doctor this styled!"
He brought out a cannon (the kind for a fort),
Aimed it directly at my poor little wart.

The blast shook the building! The smoke filled the air!
When it cleared, I looked down at my thumb, lying there—
The wart was still with me, all smug and all pink,
But my *thumb* had gone missing (a terrible link).

So the moral, dear children, is simple, it's plain:
When fighting small problems, use methods more sane.
For the wart's still attached to a thumb on the floor,
While *I've* got a stump that's now wart-free... and sore.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a silly narrative poem about a boy named Willie whose doctor tries wild and escalating remedies to remove a wart, culminating in a surprising, funny ending?
counterfactuals.output:
# Willie's Wart

Willie had a wart, you see,
Upon his knobby knee,
It sat there like a tiny king
Refusing to break free.

He went to Doctor Quibblesworth,
A man of great renown,
Who peered at Willie's troublesome bump
And gave a thoughtful frown.

"We'll paint it!" said the doctor first,
With purple iodine.
The wart just winked (or seemed to wink)
And said, "This spot is mine!"

"We'll freeze it!" cried the doctor next,
With canisters of ice.
The wart just shivered, settled in,
And thought the cold was nice.

"We'll burn it!" yelled the doctor then,
With lasers, zaps, and fire.
The wart just tanned a golden brown
And rose a half-inch higher.

"We'll starve it!" howled the doctor, wild,
With bandages of tape.
The wart grew fat on darkness, though,
And changed its very shape.

The doctor tried a hundred things—
Snake oil, chants, and spells,
Garlic wrapped in moonlit cloth,
And ringing silver bells.

He brought in wizards, brought in priests,
A witch from Timbuktu,
Who looked at Willie's knee and said,
"I've never seen one grow!"

For growing was exactly what
That wart had gone and done,
It now was big as Willie's head—
A wart-astrophic one!

The doctor wept, threw up his hands,
"I've failed you, Willie, son!
There's nothing more that I can try,
My rope has come undone!"

But Willie, calm, just shrugged and smiled,
"Don't fret, good doctor, please—
I've named him Bartholomew,
We're comfortable, at ease."

"He does my homework, tells great jokes,
He's really quite a friend,
I rather think I'll miss him when
This wart-y tale must end."

So Willie kept his wart named Bart,
They're never seen apart,
The moral here, if there must be:
Some things just win your heart!
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lighthearted but dark comedic poem in AABB rhyme scheme about a foot doctor trying every method imaginable—from tools to explosives—to remove a wart, with an unexpected outcome for the patient.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wart That Wouldn't Quit

Dr. Foote was known throughout the land,
For treating feet with steady hand,
But one wart came, a stubborn guest,
That put his skills to ultimate test.

"A simple thing," he first proclaimed,
With acid drops he'd get it tamed,
He dabbed and waited, day by day,
The wart just laughed and chose to stay.

He brought out scalpels, sharp and bright,
And carved away with all his might,
He froze it next with liquid cold,
The wart said "No" and held its hold.

He tried a laser, tried a drill,
The wart remained upon the heel,
He read of methods, quite obscure,
Consulted texts on ancient cure.

By week three, Doc had lost his cool,
He'd tried each trick, each dermal tool,
"Enough!" he cried, eyes wild with rage,
"I'll blast you off this mortal stage!"

He rigged some dynamite with care,
(The patient, understandably, showed fear)
"Just hold real still," the doctor said,
"This might get loud—perhaps see a medic instead?"

The patient fled out through the door,
Wart still attached as e'er before,
But tripped and fell down the stairs, poor soul,
And broke his foot—achieved his goal!

For in the cast, all wrapped in white,
The wart, ignored, gave up the fight,
It shriveled, dried, and slipped away,
No blast required—just an ordinary day.

Moral: sometimes when you desperately grope
For answers wrapped in dynamite and hope,
The universe, with dark comedic art,
Solves problems while you fall apart.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a whimsical poem for kids that escalates in absurdity, about treating a wart with things like hammers, drills, and dynamite, ending with an ironic twist about the patient instead of the wart.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Wart That Wouldn't Quit

I had a wart upon my thumb,
A stubborn, bumpy, bothersome one.
So Grandpa said, "I'll fix that quick!"
And grabbed his hammer, gave a *THWICK!*

The wart just giggled, "Missed me, friend!"
So Dad brought out the power drill—
He *whirred* and *buzzed* with steely will,
The wart just spun around with glee,
"That tickles! Do it more!" said he.

We tried a saw, we tried a torch,
We tried to catapult it off the porch.
We coated it in cheese and glue,
We fed it to a kangaroo,
Who spit it back and said, "No thanks,
That thing belongs with tanks and tanks!"

So Uncle Rick, in army boots,
Brought in the *dynamite* recruits.
"Stand back!" he hollered. "Cover your ears!"
We waited through our nervous tears—

## KA-BLAMMO!

Smoke cleared up, the dust settled down,
We searched the yard, we searched the town.
The wart? Still there, still snug, still small,
Just winking at us, having a ball.

But me? Oh dear, oh what a sight—
My hair was gone. My teeth felt light.
My eyebrows sat clear 'cross the street.
My shoes blew off my dizzy feet.

The doctor came and shook her head,
"The wart's just fine," is all she said.
"But YOU, my friend, need medical care—
You've quite literally lost your hair!"

So here's my tale, a lesson clear:
That little wart's still sitting here.
It's tough as nails, it will not budge—
But *I'm* the one who needs a nudge

To the hospital, in bandage wrap,
While the wart just takes a victory nap.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
